newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers stumble on EMU budget pact details.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers stumble on EMU budget pact details.

text.p: European Union finance ministers remained deadlocked Monday over a critical aspect of a new system for ensuring that states in a single currency, planned for 1999, maintain budgetary discipline after joining.

EU diplomats said there was disagreement over a precise definition of a severe recession that would allow a government to avoid sanctions if the downturn caused a deterioration of its public finances.
"There has been no significant progress," said one EU diplomat, adding that the ministers had moved on to consider the size of fines on governments running excessive deficits under the budget pact.
It was unclear whether the ministers would return to the subject of "exceptional and temporary" circumstances, the diplomat added.
Germany and the Netherlands want the definition to include a 2 percent decline in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over four consecutive quarters.
Others argued that such a strict interpretation would ignore the substantive economic differences within the 15-nation bloc.
The effort to secure a budget stability pact has become one of the most difficult hurdles in nailing down a blueprint for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Under a proposed plan, countries running annual deficits above 3 percent of GDP could face stiff fines if they failed to curb expenditure.
But if a government could show that a severe recession was behind the deterioration of its public finances, it might be able to avoid sanctions.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect behind the stability pact, arrived at the meeting late this afternoon when the talks shifted to the stability pact.
Earlier in the day, ministers were cautiously optimistic that the differences over the budget pact could be resolved. But most stopped short of making any firm predictions.

Expressing the view of many EU ministers, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit should be made after a proper evaluation of a country's economic circumstances.
"France's position is simple and clear. It is up to the (finance ministers) to decide on a case-by-case basis," Arthuis said in a newspaper interview published Monday.
Taking a shot at Germany's tough bargaining stance, Arthuis added, "When you're in a community you have to try to reach a consensus rather than imposing your point of view."

Separately, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, said he would make sure that the British government would reserve judgment on any political decision made on Monday in order to allow scrutiny by the British Parliament.

On negotiations over the legal framework for monetary union, Clarke said he secured a change in proposed legislation that would not bind any countries not participating in the common currency in 1999.

The result of Monday's talks will form the basis for discussions among EU leaders at a summit in Dublin on Dec. 13 and 14. Should they fail to resolve their differences the best that could be hoped for is a progress report, diplomats said.

The ministers are also expected to agree a blueprint for a new Exchange Rate Mechanism that will link the single currency to those of EU nations not participating among the first wave of countries in 1999.
